To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
sheep and cattle fed the same HC diets absorbed the same amount of amino acids on an equal metabolic weight basis.

the portal venous concentration and net portal amino acid absorption rates are similar for sheep and cattle fed alfalfa hay or 85% concentrate diets, with the exception of histidine and 3-methylistidine, where net portal absorption was lower in cattle.
the net portal appearance rate of amino acids was qualitatively similar between steers and sheep.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of dietary protein on amino acid absorption and metabolism in cattle and sheep.
the effect of diet on amino acids absorption in cattle and sheep.
the influence of diet and species on the absorption and metabolism of amino acids in ruminants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NPAAA rate is qualitatively and, with the exception of a few amino acids, quantitatively similar for sheep and cattle.
cattle and sheep have similar portal plasma flow rates, but that cattle and sheep differ in their portal venous- arterial concentration differences and NPAAA rates for some amino acids.
the effect of diet on the portal absorption of amino acids is minimal in sheep or cattle.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the net portal absorption rates for amino acids are similar between sheep and steers when expressed per kg of metabolic body size.
the portal amino acid profile in sheep is more sensitive to dietary manipulation than in steers, but the net absorption of amino acids in sheep and cattle is similar.

cattle and sheep are similar in their capacity to absorb amino acids from the small intestine, but cattle have a higher portal plasma flow rate than sheep and thus a higher rate of amino acid absorption.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the net absorption of amino acids is not altered by diet in cattle or sheep, but that the concentrations of amino acids in plasma are altered by diet.
cattle have a higher portal flow rate and a lower plasma flow corrected portal amino acid extraction rate than sheep.
cattle and sheep have similar portal amino acid kinetics.
